deck: 1 Introduction to Legal Systems
chap: Introduction to Legal Systems
Front: How is law an allocative system?
Back:
- Legal decisions are by nature
economic, as they allocate scarce goods and services. The legal system is
a rationing system that reflects the distribution of power in society.

- The allocation takes into
account the following factors:

- Need: (prioritise large and low
income families)

- Merit (beauty, wisdom, virtue)

- Ascriptive/Status (Birth, Sex,
Religion, Income, etc.)

- Chance (Luck)

- Lottery (Equality of
Opportunity)

- Constitutional (Determines the
way decisions are made)

deck: 2 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
Back:
- appointed by President in discussion with PM
- Ministers can have multiple portfolios
- Ministries may have 2 ministers covering different aspects (e.g. in 2016 MOE had Ong Ye Kung for higher edu and skills, Ng Chee Meng for schools)
- assisted by other MPs and Civil servants in their ministries
- 2nd rank: Minister of State
- 3rd rank: Parliamentary Secretaries (MPs)
- Ministers also have oversight over the various statutory boards which come under the purview of their respective ministries
- Statutory boards not staffed by civil servants hence not constrianed by civil service rules
- Stat boards are managed by Board of Directors which have greater independence and flexibility in their operations e.g. HDB, CPF

deck: 2 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1

- Power to appoint PM, declare PM office vacant (if PM resigns or if President is satisfied that PM has lost confidence of majority of MPs), withhold assent to dissolve parliament
- power to veto appointment of key appointment holders
- power to veto govt supply bills & all fiscal matters touching on SG's reserves
- gatekeeper role in decisions under Internal Security Act and Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act
- Require Council of Presidential Advisors' agreement before veto can be used
- Parliament can overrule President's decision with 2/3 majority vote
- Ceremonial role, support charitable causes
- chosen by popular election

- dual role of the AG
- SG's chief legal advisor - functions as the Govt's lawyer (internal affairs, civil and legislation divisions)
- Public Prosecutor - decides the course of action independently from the govt (Prosecutions division)
- Walter Woon says double role is controversial, better to split the 2 e.g. MinLaw be govt's legal advisor and AGC solely prosecutes

deck: 2 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1

- a series of laws and regulations on trade, jurisdiction and other issues
- attempted to create a modus vivendi (ideal balance) between English law & local customary traditions (on property rights, marriage and other Asian society norms)
- setting up of Registry of Land and no transfer would be recognised as valid until registered
- conduct of affairs of port of SG
- magistracy of 12 magistrates from British merchants were set up to try minor criminal and civil cases
- setting up of Resident's Court and Magistrates' Court
- native chiefs permitted to settle disputes amongst their people, subject to control of Magistracy (recognised gaps between local and English laws)

deck: 2 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1

- Raffles' Magistracy abolished, replaced with Court of Requests and Resident's court

deck: 2 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1

- Temenggong ceded control of SG to the British

deck: 2 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 1
Back:
- Applies to the Straits Settlements, comprised of Penang, Malacca and SG
- established Court of Judicature for Straits Settlements in Penang. Consisted of Governor, Resident Councillors, and legally trained Recorder
- CoJ same jurisdiction as High Court and Court of Chancery in UK
- English law to be applied, and modified in application according to the local circumstances
- Criminal: administered English law with due attention given to local customs and religions
- Civil: judgment and sentences given according to "justice and right"
- unsuitable statute/case not received as part of SG law
- constitution: past laws would continue in force, subject to modifications to suit local needs
- Legislations existing in 1826 England also transferred to SG, no English statute passed after 1826 became SG law except for mercantile law (S5 of CLA, repealed in 1993)
- Presidency of Straits
Settlements formed with Robert Fullerton as Governor
- Powers to make law vested with the Supreme Government in
India, and British Parliament.
- Governor Fullerton later closed the courts
temporarily, leading to legal chaos

SG, as long as it was part of the law of SG immediately before 12 Nov 1993.
- Section 3 (2): Common law and equity will continue to
be in force, as long as it is applicable to Singapore’s circumstances. Judges

bound by the English Privy Council, or its own past decisions.

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: Why does SG parliament only have 1 house?
Back:
- SG too small
- separate chambers would be too divisive
- upper chamber might become the mouthpiece of a minority party
- second chamber would be severely critcised if it thwarted the will of the majority, as expressed through elected representatives
- difficulties in finding suitable candidates

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: How do candidates become part of Parliament?
Back:
Singapore’s legislature consisted of representatives voted
into office by popular vote under the single plurality first past the post
system.

Person securing the most number of votes in Constituency thus declared
to become members of parliament

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
■ SG citizen

■ At least 21 years old

■ Resident of SG at the time of
nomination

■ Of sound mind and able to
actively take part in debate in Parliament

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
- Legislative power vested in parliament - makes bills, amendments to law i.e. govern all aspects of lives
- debates the govt budget of respective ministries. ability to scrutinise, clarify and challenge govt policies

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
Very strict
- no one votes against govt lines, members of a particular party will loyally vote according to the party's dictates
- members who vote against their own party's policies etc will be dealt with by the party's disciplinarian, the whip. he may lose his party membership and hence his seat in Parliament

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: Why are private members' bills extremely rare?
Back:
■ As ruling PAP has continuously been in
power since 1959, no real opportunity for its backbenches to introduce new
legislation of their own since the party is already in power

■ At both formulation and actual law-making
stages, MPs assume a more muted and passive role

■ MPs lack legislative initiative and almost
all legislation comes from the Cabinet acting on its own initiative or on the
advice of senior civil servants

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2

Back:
- ensure minority representation in parliament
- efficiently manage SG's public housing estates

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Front: What are the weaknesses of the GRC scheme?
Back:
- constant enlargement of GRCs and shifting of political boundaries made it very difficult for opposition parties to get a foothold in GEs. ethnic minority and 3 to 6 member requirement made it difficult for opposition parties to contest due to their small size
- Electoral boundaries commission, which report directly to the PM's ofice, draws the constituency boundaries before a GE (gerrymandering)
- Most opposition parties lacked recognisable
personalities to helm their GRC teams, unlike the PAP, who strategically placed
well-known cabinet ministers as leaders of their GRC teams

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2

- picked from parties whose members were not members of govt
- increased from 3 to 6 to 9
- now max 12 NCMPs can be picked to set a minimum number of opp MPs
- 1st NCMP after 1984 GE: Dr Lee Siew Choh of WP

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
From 1984 to 2017, NCMPs can only debate on parliamentary issues. Prohibited from voting on constitutional amendments, supply bills and motions of confidence on the govt

In 2016, Article 38 of the constitution was amended to allow NCMPs to vote on all bills after 2017. Same voting rights as MPs as NCMP have as much mandate as MPs

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2

- offer an alternative voice in the parliament through opp party members that are not elected
- keep govt on its toes
- quell Singaporeans' desire to elect an alternative party into power

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2

- Lacked legitimacy
- 3/99 seats for NCMPs too small to make a difference
- Public likened it to tokenism
- NCMPs get no support from parliament to engage assistance to help them in their work

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
chap: Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2
Back:
Include alternative, non-partisan voices in parliament which could add to the variety of
view during parliamentary debate and raise the tenure of debate in the House
- sought to break the polarisation between the ruling and opposition parties
- Improves the quality of parliamentary
debates by bringing alternative voices to the Parliament as NMPs are experts in their field

- NMPs can argue and reason in parliamentary
debates without having to be bound to their political party's control

deck: 3 Development of SG's Legal & Constitution System 2

deck: 8 The Anatomy of a Criminal Trial

Front: Goals of the criminal justice system
Back:
Goals of the Criminal Justice
System

●
Seek and achieve justice, not merely to convict

○
Any miscarriage of justice would diminish the standing of
both the Court and the Prosecution in the eyes of the public

○
Judges should allow accused to plead to their charges and
sentence them in a fair manner

○
This attitude can be seen in when the accused has requested
for a short delay in the commencement of the sentence

○
Even the perpetrator of the most heinous crime deserves
fair treatment under the law

●
Should take consistent institutional view on cases of law
about the same kind of issues

○
To ensure that all accused persons are treated fairly and
equally, be it before the court or at the stage when the Prosecution decides
whether or not to charge an offender

●
Retribution

●
Rehabilitation of the guilty party

●
For lawyers to act in the best interest of their clients

○
A criminal lawyers should not approach any case with
preconceived notions and should maintain an open mind and consider all
available defences, however obscure

●
Ethical conduct of the lawyers

○
The accused, the court and the community are entitled to
expect that in performing his function in presenting the case against an
accused person, the Prosecutor will act with fairness and detachment with the
sole and unadulterated objective to establish the whole truth in accordance
with the law

○
Prosecution ought to remember that their ethical duty to
act in the interest of justice must always take precedence over whatever
pressures or incentives they have to “win” by securing a conviction

●
Truth finding

○
A court will decide on the basis of the evidence presented
to it, whether a person accused in a criminal case should be convicted or
acquitted

●
Evidence is necessary to ascertain the truth of the
circumstances because facts are disputed

deck: 8 The Anatomy of a Criminal Trial
chap: The Anatomy of a Criminal Trial
Back:
●
The
accused is presumed innocent and that is for the Prosecution to prove his guilt
beyond reasonable doubt

○
The impact of this presumption on truth depends on the extent
to which the innocent party is able to garner sufficient admissible evidence,
which is ultimately dependent on his resources, the state of the evidence and
the skill of his lawyer

○
Allegations must be founded upon admissible evidence

■
This prevents there being speculation about the accused and
their crime

■
And ensures that any criminal charges are founded by logic
and facts, and not just mere exaggerations or false statements

deck: 8 The Anatomy of a Criminal Trial

Back: To do right by the public, by ensuring that the streets are kept safe and criminals are punished for their errors

- have to get the witnesses to speak about what has happened

- DC can submit that the prosecution has no case or establish D's case

The adversarial system assumes the best way to get to the

application of the law accurately

○
Seeks to achieve this purpose by placing the court in an
optimal position to accurately adjudicate the case through a process governed
by a body of rules which

(1) Control the scope of information (evidence) put before
the court so it may effectively adjudicate the dispute between the parties

(2) Prescribe the mode or manner in which evidence is to be
presented so as to facilitate assessment by the court

(3) Define the obligation of the parties to prove, through
the evidence presented, the facts which they assert

deck: 8 The Anatomy of a Criminal Trial
chap: The Anatomy of a Criminal Trial
Front: Factors that compromise the court's ability to adjudicate accurately
Back:
(1) For example, a witness may successfully lie or exaggerate
the evidence or give a favourable impression which has no basis in
reality.

(2) As the efficacy of the process of cross-examination
depends on the circumstances of the case, and the skill and the preparation of
the lawyer who questions the witness, there is no guarantee that it will
achieve its purposes.

(3) Truth may also be compromised by the technicality and
complexity of the law.

(4) The judicial inquiry is weakened by its
dependence on second hand information of past events. The judge has to rely on
inferior information and the best that he can do is determine the extent to
which the evidence put before the court should be believed.

○ Participation in politicised law reform
activities

■ E.g. constitutional challenges, class
action lawsuits

● Advantage:

○ More proactive role in ensuring justice

○ Persuading clients to do the right thing

● Disadvantage:

○ Tendency to place the lawyer’s ideals above
the client’s interests

○ Neglecting the principle that anyone should
be entitled to legal representation

deck: 11 Access to Justice
chap: Access to Justice
Front: Why no cause lawyering in SG?
Back:
○ Operation Coldstore
established 3 thematic pillars of SG political life

■ State’s capacity to deploy
detention without trial against political opponents

■ State’s capacity to
characterise political opponents as threats

■ State’s capacity to
characterise critique as a form or political opposition endangering the
‘nation’

○ Mass Media heavily regulated

deck: 11 Access to Justice
chap: Access to Justice
Back:
● Defined by general principles of ethics

● Focuses
on preserving relationships and minimising harm

○ Addresses concrete needs of all parties

○ Ensures that only those that can best bear
harm will receive harm

○ Goal-directed (teleological) view of
relationships

● Advantage:

○ Emphasises dialogue between lawyers and
clients

○ Looks for non-adversarial ways to resolve
disputes

● Disadvantage:

○ May ignore justice in certain situations
(e.g. domestic abuse)
○ Highly conservative and may not address social and
political injustice

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- Set of rules generally regarded and
accepted as binding between states
- Fundamental principles still remain from
traditions from the 19th century

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
● Exercised within a single jurisdiction (may
be a state)

● Exercised with full sovereignty

○ Government exercises full legislative power

● Laws in Singapore are mostly municipal in
their effect and operation

○ Exceptions of extra-territorial laws such as
Prevention of Corruption Act

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
●
General Assembly of United Nations – Legislative

●
International Court of Justice – Judicial

●
UN Security Council/Interpol – Executive

Note that they do not act exactly like
their municipal counterparts: e.g. judicial adjudication only applies if both
parties agree to consult it, unlike municipal where one party can compel the
other against its will to attend court

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- international conventions/treaties
- binding contracts between states
- can involve reporting requirements
- signature: mere acknowledgement of treaty
- ratification: bound to terms of treaty after govt is conulted
- accession: same legal effect as ratification, but not preceded by signature and usually for already existing treaties
- customary international law
- practice of states not written but regarded as legally binding, may be codified in treaties
- Jus Cogens or peremptory norms

- Fundamental
CIL that no derogation is permitted

- Any
law that conflicts with these laws are considered null and void

- Rooted
in natural principles

- E.g.
no torture, wars of aggression, genocide, crimes against humanity

- general principles of law recognised by civilised nations

- judicial decisions and the writings of the most highly qualified publicists

- decisions by ICJ, permanent court of international justice etc

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
● States already chose to
comply with these laws as they are within their interests

● Obligatory force of
international law (easier to follow the norm rather than go against it)

● Caution of individuals

○ Most individual actors are
civil servants who hope to be promoted or avoid being sacked

○ Incentive to follow
international law

● Consistency of behaviour
(following international law) is highly prized on the international stage (to
maintain relations with other states, which has impacts on other areas)

● These justifications are
less compelling for non-state actors

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
● No tribunal has compulsory
jurisdiction

● Parties agree to be judged under the rules of
the tribunal

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
● Established in 1945 after WW2

● 6 Principal Organs

● Singapore joined in September 1965 as the 117th
member

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
● General Assembly

○ Deliberative body

○ Involves all UN members

○ Decides on admission of new members/elects members to UN security
council etc.

● Security Council

○ Responsible for promotion of international peace and security

○ 15 members – 10 elected, 5 permanent members with all-powerful
veto power

■ The 5 permanent members are US, China, UK, France and Russia.

○ Power to establish peacekeeping operations, impose international
sanctions, and authorise military action through its resolutions

○ The only body whose resolutions are binding on all other member
states

● Economic and Social
Council (ECOSOC)

○ Body for deliberation of global economic and social affairs

○ Coordinates work of UN’s numerous specialized agencies

■ E.g. WHO

○ 4 members elected by assembly

● Secretariat

○ Administrative arm

○ Supports work of UN and all its bodies

○ Headed by UN Secretary-general, elected by general assembly

● International Court of
Justice (ICJ)

○ Judicial arm

○ Main dispute resolution body for UN’s members

○ Does not have compulsory jurisdiction over all members of the UN

○ Optional jurisdiction – States can choose whether to bring case
to the ICJ

■ E.g. Pedra Branca

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- initiative: Forum of small states
- small-5 initiative:
- Includes Costa Rica, Jordan, Liechtenstein,
Singapore and Switzerland

- Works to improve UN Security Council’s
operations and increase involvement of non-UNSC members in its work

- Global governance group (3G): breach widening gap between actions & deliberations of G20 countries and other states
- UN peacekeeping operations
- 1990 Iraq-Kuwait Observer Mission

- June 1991 UN Angola Verification Mission II and UN mission in Western Sahara

- 31 March 1992 UN Transitionary Authority in
Cambodia

- September 1999 UN Multi-National Force for East Timor

- SG & ASEAN's role in condemning the Vietnamese invasion of Cambodia: Argued that it was
the lesser of two evils to allow the representative of the murderous Khmer
Rouge regime to keep its seat and uphold the principle of territorial
sovereignty and inviolability

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- small states like SG need to negotiate ASAP
- Decisions on the signing
or accession to treaties is made by the Cabinet who will then delegate the
Ministry of Foreign Affairs to work out the technical details.

- MFA has no legal
division and works with the International Affairs Division (IAD) of the
Attorney-General’s Chambers
- Examine if it would
bring changes to any part of our domestic law

- Examine if the
legislation needs to be changed to comply with these terms.

- Where the treaties allow
for something or require a declaration etc. – it would shape the way in
which the country chooses to become a member of that treaty

- other considerations
- nature of the consent the state is given
- timing of the act of consent (have to accede if signature/ratification time has closed)
- signature (not full consent, need to ratify to be bound)

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
● The dualist approach views international and
municipal law as two distinct sets of legal orders

o (vs.
monist system – where international and local law system are the same; when you
sign an international treaty it automatically becomes part of local law)

● Singapore adopts a monist approach towards Customary
International Law

● Singapore adopts a dualist
approach towards the application of
treaties .All
treaty obligations are met by

· Existing
legislature or

· transformative
legislation. (Creating New Legislature or changing existing legislature)

E.g. We acceded to the Convention Preventing or
Prohibiting Genocide in 1995 but it didn’t become part of Singapore law till
2007, when it was incorporated into the Penal Code.

● This is in line with the Doctrine of Incorporation: Even after
accession – a treaty is only applicable if parliament enacts a law that applies
it. A treaty is not self-executing/automatically applicable – it has to
come into the intermediation of domestic law

○ There may be a kind of
contextualising and codification of international law, to adapt to the local
context.

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- treaty law: contract between states
- CIL: need SG's judicial recognition to apply, must align with state practice
- 2-Step Inquiry for CIL

(1) Ascertain whether it
is actually a CIL or merely a political claim? (Ascertain legal status)

(2) Determine
how can it be applied to Singapore, and how it is relevant on the facts

· E.g. Yong Vui Kong (2010):
Court felt that although torture was a CIL, death by hanging was not CIL

o Issue of Hierarchy – it matters whether the CIL enters
at the level of common law, statutory law, or constitutional law.

· E.g.
Using the same example of the death penalty, if the CIL enters at the common
law, the Misuse of Drugs Act can still trump it VS if it came in at the
constitutional law level – it would be more likely the CIL will stand.

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Front: Legislative measures to implement international law
Back:
● Where economic initiatives
are concerned (eg. trade), the government aims to align with international
standards by using binding legislation
to attain legal harmonisation

○ Eg. The 2010 Electronics
Transactions Act was enacted to implement the UN Convention on the Use of
Electronic Communications in International Contracts

● To accommodate cultural
and religious minority rights, Singapore has made reservations to various human
rights treaties

○ Eg. Gender equality laws
in relation to the Administration of Muslim Law Act are immunised from the
Convention on the Elimination of All Forms of Discrimination against Women
(“CEDAW”)

● This truncates the
transformative impact treaties might otherwise have on domestic law

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Front: Non-binding measures to implement international law
Back:
● However, the government
prefers to adopt non-binding guidelines to implement international treaties.

● This is especially so for
those relating to human rights or labour law – preference for making policy
rather than legal amendments

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
The Court is permitted to look at all
manner of extra-legislative material, including international treaties and
agreements to aid in interpretation
- Domestic statutes prevail over CIL norms
- SG will try as far as possible to interpret domestic law consistently with SG's intl legal obligations
- Where a statute refers to
any treaty or international agreement, section 9A(3) of the Interpretation Act
(Cap 1) permits reference to this to assist in interpreting statutory
provisions. (i.e. they may refer to the definition used in the treaty).

- Changes can be made to
international treaties when adopting it in the local context. Parliament in
enacting legislation to give effect to treaties may include provisions which go beyond treaty terms, which will
prevail where the wording is clear.

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- Cases involving
international law and the exercise of executive prerogative powers are immune
from review as they are considered matters of policy. This is due to the need
for the separation of powers and requires deference to the executive branch.
- However, International treaties which have been
incorporated into the domestic legal order may be reviewed.

deck: 12 SG & the International Legal System
chap: SG & the International Legal System
Back:
- Sg vulnerable as small state, need intl law to preserve sovereignty
- having intl law better than no law to restrain big powers - intl law may provide the only bulwark against naked, raw power and brute force
- ensures that we coexist by not attacking others and to cooperate to a certain extent
- SG championed the settlement of disputes through peaceful negotiations/3rd party adjudication e.g. Pedra Blanca dispute with Malaysia brought to ICJ for a fair and just decision by international courts
